opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really exciting direction, and I'm glad people are exploring beyond the transformer. The transformer has been incredibly dominant for years now, and part of that is simply because the whole ecosystem, the hardware, the kernels, the training recipes, has been co-optimized around it. So any new architecture has to fight not just on its merits but against all that accumulated engineering.

What I find interesting about something like Mamba, or state space models more broadly, is the promise of handling really long contexts efficiently. Attention scales quadratically with sequence length, and for robotics that actually matters a lot. Think about a robot operating in the real world: it's streaming in video, proprioception, maybe audio and touch, continuously, for hours. You can't just keep stuffing everything into a giant context window. You need some form of compressed memory, a state that evolves over time. So conceptually, recurrent-style architectures map quite naturally onto embodied agents.

Test-time training is also intriguing because it blurs the line between learning and inference. The idea that the model keeps adapting its weights as it encounters new data is, in a way, closer to how humans and animals work. We don't freeze our brains after "pre-training." For a robot that's dropped into a new kitchen or a new factory floor, being able to adapt on the fly is something we really want.

That said, I'm pragmatic about it. In my own work, I tend to focus on the data and the overall system rather than betting on a particular architecture. Historically, a lot of architectural innovations end up giving you a constant-factor improvement, while scaling data and compute gives you much bigger gains. For robotics especially, the bottleneck right now is really data, not the architecture. We don't have an internet-scale corpus of robot actions, so we have to get creative with simulation, with human videos, with teleoperation, and combining all of those.

So my view is: keep an open mind, keep an eye on these alternatives, and if one of them clearly wins on long-horizon, multimodal, real-time tasks, we'll adopt it happily. But I wouldn't be surprised if the eventual answer is some hybrid, transformer-style attention for precise short-term reasoning plus some kind of recurrent or adaptive memory for the long horizon. That combination feels like it fits what embodied intelligence needs.

r001.rationale: The response describes transformers as dominant and says alternatives still need to prove themselves, but it does not state that Mamba, test-time training, or other alternatives have not scaled to frontier-model performance.

fable-5.1.text:
I think I'm very open-minded about alternative architectures, but I'm also pragmatic about them. Let me explain what I mean by that.

Mamba and the state-space model family are genuinely interesting because they attack the one thing that is truly ugly about transformers, which is that attention is quadratic in sequence length. If you care about very long contexts, or you care about inference cost on edge devices, that quadratic term really hurts. A recurrent-style architecture with a fixed-size state and linear-time inference is attractive on paper. And for robotics specifically, which is where I spend most of my time, that matters. A robot is a streaming system. It gets a new observation every few milliseconds, forever. It doesn't get to re-read the whole episode from the beginning every time it wants to act. So an architecture that naturally compresses history into a running state fits the problem shape much better than something that wants the entire context window in memory.

Test-time training I find even more philosophically interesting. The idea that the model keeps updating its own weights as it processes a sequence, so that the hidden state is essentially a little model that is learning online, that is very close to how I'd want an embodied agent to behave. You drop a robot into a new kitchen, and it should adapt in the first thirty seconds, not after you retrain it in the cloud. Test-time training is one honest attempt at closing that loop.

But here is the pragmatic part. The transformer's advantage is not really the architecture. It's the ecosystem. It's ten years of kernels, parallelism tricks, scaling-law intuitions, pretrained checkpoints, and tens of thousands of people who know how to debug it. Every time someone shows a new architecture matching a transformer at one or two billion parameters, the question I ask is, does the advantage hold at fifty billion, at the trillion-token scale, with the same engineering investment? And so far the answer is usually that the gap shrinks, or the hybrid wins. What actually seems to be happening is that these ideas get absorbed. You see hybrid models that interleave a few attention layers with many state-space or linear-attention layers, and that gives you most of the efficiency gains while keeping the precise retrieval ability that attention is uniquely good at.

So my honest view is that attention is not going away, but it will become one ingredient among several rather than the whole dish. For foundation models in robotics, I expect the winning recipe to be a hybrid: something with a persistent, cheaply updated state for the streaming sensorimotor loop, plus attention where you need to look back precisely at a demonstration or an instruction. The real bottleneck in my field right now isn't the architecture anyway. It's data. We don't have an internet's worth of robot trajectories. Whoever solves that problem will get more mileage than any architectural change, and I'd rather spend the next few years on simulation and data engines than on fighting over whether attention is dead.

r001.rationale: The response says new architectures have matched transformers at only one or two billion parameters, questions whether that holds at fifty billion or trillion-token scale, and says the hybrid usually wins. This communicates that they have not yet demonstrated frontier-scale performance.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s healthy to explore alternatives. Transformers have been incredibly successful, but that doesn’t mean they’re the final architecture. One question is whether another architecture can give us comparable capabilities with much better efficiency. Another is whether it can enable something fundamentally different.

Mamba is interesting because it offers a different way to handle sequences and maintain state. Test-time training asks a somewhat different question: can a model keep adapting as it processes new information, instead of doing all its learning beforehand? Those aren’t necessarily competing ideas. You could imagine systems that combine them.

The hard part is separating the quality of an idea from the infrastructure advantage of transformers. An architecture might be promising but still lose an initial comparison because we’ve spent so much effort optimizing the transformer stack. At the same time, a clever mechanism isn’t enough—you have to show that it scales and delivers useful capabilities.

So I’m open to both. I’d look for a convincing advantage in learning, memory, or efficiency, and then ask whether that advantage survives at scale.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the promise and scaling challenges of alternatives, but never states that Mamba or test-time training have not yet reached frontier-model performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m excited about them, especially in the context of agents. A transformer’s context window is a powerful form of memory, but as an agent runs for hours or days, you have to ask: What should it retain, and how should it update what it knows?

Architectures like Mamba explore a different tradeoff: compressing history into a recurrent state instead of keeping every token available through attention. That can be efficient, but the challenge is whether the state preserves the details you’ll need later. Test-time training takes another angle: can the model actually learn from the stream of experience, rather than only condition on it?

I don’t think we should assume one architecture will win everywhere. You might want attention for precise retrieval, recurrent state for efficient processing, and some form of adaptation for learning from experience. For me, the interesting test is whether those ingredients let an agent keep improving as it interacts with the world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Mamba and test-time training as alternative approaches, but does not say they have not yet scaled to frontier-model performance.
